newsitem.title: ECUADOR: At least one protester killed in Ecuador crisis.
newsitem.headline: At least one protester killed in Ecuador crisis.

text.p: At least one person was killed in disturbances outside Ecuador's presidential palace on Friday as ousted president Abdala Bucaram defied a growing chorus of calls for his removal.
The disturbances erupted after Fabian Alarcon, the congressional leader named interim head of state on Thursday, urged about 4,000 anti-Bucaram demonstrators to take the palace by force.

Hundreds of riot police, backed by armoured personnel carriers and water cannon, fired repeated volleys of tear gas into the protesters as they sought to breech police lines around the palace and Quito's historic Independence Plaza.

At least six people were injured in the ensuing melee, as protesters fought back with rocks and homemade gasoline bombs, and police said 18-year-old student Patricio Uyumbillo died of unknown causes. But opposition politicans and witnesses said the youth's skull was crushed by a teargas canister.

Sporadic disturbances were reported all day in the colonial streets around the Carondelet palace. But the pitched battles and dense plumes of tear gas that engulfed the downtown area late on Friday were the worst since irate Ecuadoreans rose up against a hard-hitting package of economic austerity measures last month.
Police also used tear gas to break up violent disturbances on Friday in the Pacific coast city of Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city.
The unrest in both cities came despite the embattled government's declaration of a state of emergency rule and the suspension of individual guarantees early on Friday.

Apart from the acrid smell of tear gas, the streets of this Andean capital were awash with coup rumours, which reached a fever pitch after armed forces chief Gen. Paco Moncayo met Bucaram and his vice president, Rosalia Arteaga, for nearly two hours on Friday evening.

A defence ministry source said Moncayo had thrown the army's weight behind Arteaga, who has declared herself Bucaram's legitimate successor. But Bucaram emerged from the meeting saying the military was "monolithic" in its support of Ecuador's democratic institutions and insisted that he remained fully in charge of the government.
"We looking for peace and tranquility within the constitutional framework," he said.

Critics of Bucaram, who took office just six months ago and is popularly known as "El Loco" or "madman," said he looked more like a punch drunk in a ring that was crumbling beneath him than someone who could cling to power much longer.

Government sources said Bucaram left the presidential palace late on Friday for the first time since his supposed removal from power. But the sources played down the significance, saying he was only leaving to spend Ecuador's four-day carnival weekend with his family in Guayaquil.

In Washington, the United States said it was concerned by the constitutional crisis in Ecuador and the State Department urged the political leadership in Quito to resolve its disputes peacefully and within the bounds of Ecuadoran laws.
"The continuation of this climate of uncertainty can only damage Ecuador's national interests and its standing in the community of democratic nations," it said.
